newsitem.title: USA: IMF wants Algeria reform, worried about security. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: IMF wants Algeria reform, worried about security. [CORRECTED 23:38 GMT]

text.p: Algeria must press on with reforms despite high unemployment and an acute housing problem and must resolve security issues to attract foreign investment, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday.
A statement issued after the IMF's annual review of the Algerian economy said reforms had already brought inflation down sharply but policy needed to remain tight to consolidate this.

"Recognizing that the very high levels of unemployment and the acute housing problem could be putting pressures on the social consensus for reform, (IMF) directors encouraged the authorities to intensify efforts to marshal public support to persevere with the adjustment and reform programme," it said.

"Establishing a dynamic and growing private (corrects from public) sector (is) crucial to reducing unemployment and ensuring sustainable growth... Establishing security and political stability would be an essential precondition for the foreign investment and technology transfers needed for the private sector."

An estimated 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria since the authorities scrapped the results of a poll in 1992 and decided to ban the radical Islamic Salvation Front. The violence continued after general elections last month.
The authorities said on Wednesday that local elections would be held on Oct. 23.

The IMF, which is backing Algerian reforms with a $1.6 billion three-year loan programme, said inflation had fallen to single figures -- prices rose a year-on-year eight percent in March -- from a preliminary 15.1 percent last year and 38.6 percent in 1994.
Real GDP growth was four percent last year, up from 3.9 percent in 1995 and a fall of 0.9 percent in 1994. But unemployment was 28.0 percent, barely changed from 28.1 percent in 1995.
Non-energy foreign investment was low because firms were worried about security, it said. "Security considerations have impeded foreign investment outside the hydrocarbon sector," the statement said.

But the IMF said Algeria was now better placed to realise the fundamental objectives of the IMF programme -- macroeconomic stabilisation and an outward-oriented economy driven by private-sector led growth.

It said the Algerian authorities needed to strengthen the budget, mobilising more revenue at home to offset further reductions in domestic tariffs. Monetary policies should remain tight and interest rates should stay positive.
Structural reforms should be accelerated, including decisive action on privatisation and efforts to reform the judiciary and improve labour flexibility.
